I'll start by reading the instructions, schema, and rules files.

1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.
163	
164	## Finish
165	1. Validate that your file parses as JSON.
166	2. Check every span occurs verbatim in the paper.
167	3. Check every row has every schema field.
168	4. Reply with:
169	   - the number of rows per table;
170	   - the number of individuals;
171	   - anything you were unsure how to record.

8	# Expanding the spectrum of A20 haploinsufficiency in two Chinese families: cases report

10	## Abstract
11	
12	BackgroundThe association between mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene and a new autoinflammatory disease (called A20 haploinsufficiency, HA20) has recently been recognized. Here, we describe four patients with HA20 from two unrelated Chinese families.Case presentationA total of four patients from two families were included. The average age at onset was 5.9 years. All patients had no signs of eye or skin problems, such as uveitis, rash, folliculitis and dermal abscess. Prior to the recognition of HA20, P1 was diagnosed with SLE, liver fibrosis and hypothyroidism. She also had no oral, genital or perineal ulcers. P2 was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease and inflammatory bowel disease-related arthritis (IBD-RA). He had a perianal abscess but no oral or genital ulcers. P3, the father of P1 and P2, only had mild oral ulcers, arthralgia, and archosyrinx. P4 was diagnosed with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) and interstitial lung disease (ILD). Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed in two families. WES revealed heterozygous c.559C > T in the TNFAIP3 gene in P1, P2 and P3, while the c.259C > T mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene was identified in P4. The c.259C > T mutations is novel.ConclusionHA20 had a different phenotype between families and even between family members with the same mutation. Liver fibrosis, hypothyroidism, ILD and MAS in the patients with HA20 were first reported in this study. Our results expanded the phenotype and genotype spectrum of A20 haploinsufficiency.Electronic supplementary materialThe online version of this article (10.1186/s12881-019-0856-1) contains supplementary material, which is available to authorized users.

14	## Background
15	
16	The TNFAIP3 gene that encodes the 90 kDa A20 protein was first described in 1990 as a TNF-α-induced primary response gene in endothelial cells [1]. The protein A20 is a negative regulator of the TNF-nuclear factor-kB signaling pathway, which plays fundamental roles in various physiological and pathological processes, such as immunity, apoptosis, inflammation, and cancer [2, 3]. Polymorphisms in TNFAIP3 have been linked to the development of several autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases in genome-wide association studies, such as systemic lupus erythematosus [4–6], Sjögren’s Syndrome [7], Crohn disease [8], rheumatoid arthritis [9, 10], type 1 diabetes [11] and psoriasis [12]. Recently, heterozygous germline mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene have been found to cause the haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20), which displays an early-onset autoinflammatory disease resembling Behçet’s disease [13]. HA20, first described by Zhou et al. in 2016, is a new autoinflammatory disease [13]. Zhou et al. found that the major phenotype of HA20 displays Behçet’s disease-like symptoms, including recurrent aphthous stomatitis, genital ulcers, and intestinal symptoms [13]. However, a number of studies showed that some patients present with not only the features of autoinflammatory diseases but also several autoimmune-like features [14–17]. Therefore, these preceding clinical reports suggested that there might be unexpected phenotypes in HA20. Cases with HA20 were not reported in China. In this study, we described four patients in two HA20 families, which were diagnosed by whole exons sequencing, to enrich the phenotype and genotype spectrum of HA20.
17	
18	## Case presentation
19	
20	Two unrelated families with HA20 were enrolled in this study (Fig. 1). All adults provided written informed consent.

24	### Family 1
25	
26	The proband 1 (P1), a 14-year-old Chinese girl, presented with abdominal swelling at the age of 7. She went to her local hospital, and ultrasound showed hepatomegaly, ascites and pericardial effusion. Laboratory findings suggested dysfunction of the liver and thyroid. Therefore, hepatic fibrosis, pericardial effusion and hypothyroidism were diagnosed. She was referred to our hospital for evaluation because of the continued hepatomegaly with hepatic dysfunction for 4 years and intermittent fever for 6 months at the age of 11. Laboratory testing revealed leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hematuria, proteinuria, low levels of complement, and high levels of erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Coombs test was positive. ANA and SSA were positive, while other autoantibodies were negative. Abdominal contrast-enhanced MRI revealed hepatomegaly and hepatic fibrosis (Fig. 2a). She was diagnosed with hypothyroidism, hepatic fibrosis, systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis. Liver biopsy was performed due to continued hepatomegaly and hepatic dysfunction and showed liver fibrosis (Fig. 2b). Renal biopsy was also done because of persistent hematuria and proteinuria and displayed moderately increased mesangial matrix and mesangial hypercellularity under the light microscope; subepithelial deposits were noted, and some mesangial changes were possibly present by electron microscopy. Immunofluorescence was positive forC1q, C3, IgA, IgM, and Fb (Fig. 2c). Oral prednisolone and hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) combined with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) were given to her. Six months later, the level of complement was restored to normal, hematuria and proteinuria disappeared, and liver function returned to normal. The patient is currently receiving anti-TNFα (etanercept 25 mg/week) in combination with HCQ, low dose prednisolone and MMF. The treatment has displayed good efficacy.

30	Patient 2 (P2), the 5.1-year-old younger brother of P1, presented with a fever of unknown origin and had polyarthritis at age 2.6. He was initially diagnosed with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) because of the chronic synovitis of his joints, which was found in a local hospital (Fig. 2d). He was admitted to our hospital for further assessment due to abdominal pain, diarrhea and perianal abscess after discharge from the local hospital. On admission, HLA-B27 was positive, but no significant autoantibody was detected in his serum. Under endoscopy, multiple ulcers were found on the gastrointestinal tract. The change of pathology was consistent with Crohn’s disease. Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease and inflammatory bowel disease-related arthritis (IBD-RA). Prednisolone, Etiasa and MTX were given to him, and his joint symptoms and intestinal symptoms disappeared gradually. He is currently being treated with anti-TNFα (etanercept 12.5 mg/ 5 days), Etiasa and MTX. The treatment has displayed good efficacy.

32	Patient 3 (P3), the father of P1 and P2, also had a history of recurrent arthralgia and anal fistula starting from 7 years of age. He refused further assessment.

34	### Family 2
35	
36	Patient 4 (P4), a 9-year-old girl, visited a local hospital complaining of a fever of unknown origin and polyarthritis at the age of 7 years. She was also diagnosed with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) because of the chronic synovitis of her joints (Fig. 2e). She was referred to our hospital for evaluation due to oral ulcers, cough, and positive ANA and anti-ds DNA antibodies after discharge from the local hospital. She had no relevant past medical history and no family history of rheumatic diseases. On admission, laboratory studies showed hyperferritinemia (> 2000 ng/ml), hypertriglyceridemia (5.57 mmol/L), hypofibrinogenemia (2.0 g/L), and increased levels of Alanine Aminotransferase (61 IU/L), Glutamic-oxalacetic Transaminase (97 IU/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (726 IU/L). HLA-B27 and ANA were positive for her, but no other autoantibody was detected in her serum. Lung CT scan showed interstitial lung disease (ILD) (Fig. 2f). Therefore, she was diagnosed with JIA, macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) and ILD. Voltaren, prednisolone, and CSA were given to her, and her temperature became stable while joint symptoms disappeared quickly. She is currently receiving anti-TNFα (etanercept 25 mg/week) in association with low dose prednisolone. The treatment has displayed good efficacy, and ILD was significantly improved (Fig. 2f).

81	### Whole exome sequencing
82	
83	Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed in two HA20 families, which included all members in Fig. 1. Methodology of WES and Sanger sequencing refers to our published work [18]. An average of 11.8Gb of raw sequence data was generated with 92.65× depth of exome target regions for each individual as paired-end 150 base pair reads. 91.2% of the raw date sequencing quality was above Q30. The coverage of at least 10× and 20× of the target regions was 99.52 and 97.5% respectively.
84	
85	WES revealed heterozygous c.559C > T(p.Q187X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene (RS:NM_006290) in P1, P2 and P3, while the mutation was not detected in other members in family 1. The c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene (RS:NM_006290) was identified in P4, but the mutation was not found in her parents.
86	
87	Therefore, the c.559C > T and c.259C > T mutations were de novo for P3 and P4, respectively. No mutations were detected in other genes associated with autoinflammatory diseases (see the Additional file 1) in two families.
88	
89	### Sanger sequencing
90	
91	Sanger sequencing was used to confirm mutations identified by WES. Methodology of Sanger sequencing also refers to our published work [18]. Two mutations, c.559C > T and c.259C > T in the TNFAIP3 gene, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing in two families (Fig. 3). They were checked in mutation databases on human populations, such as ExAC Browser (http://exac.broadinstitute.org/), 1000Genomes (http://www.internationalgenome.org/), and HGMD (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/ac/index.php). The c.259C > T mutation was not found in the above mutation databases.

95	## Discussion and conclusion
96	
97	In this study, we describe the clinical manifestations of four Chinese patients with HA20 from two unrelated families. Four patients all had no signs of eye and skin problems, such as uveitis, rash, folliculitis and dermal abscess. Based on clinical features, P1 was initially diagnosed with SLE, liver fibrosis and hypothyroidism. She also had no oral, genital or perineal ulcers. P2 was initially diagnosed with Crohn’s disease and inflammatory bowel disease-related arthritis (IBD-RA). He had perianal abscess but no oral or genital ulcers. However, P3, the father of P1 and P2, only had mild oral ulcers, arthralgia, and archosyrinx. Therefore, three patients had different phenotypes in this family. Furthermore, signs of liver and thyroid problems were never reported before in HA20 patients in other studies.
98	
99	P4 was initially diagnosed with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) because of the chronic synovitis of her joints. Although ANA was positive, no other autoantibody was detected in her serum. She did not meet the classification criteria for SLE. However, she met the classification criteria of macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) in suspected systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (SJIA) due to fever, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia and hypofibrinogenemia. She had a cough, and her lung CT scan showed ILD. ILD is one of the most common and clinically important manifestations of autoimmune diseases/connective tissue disease [19]. To date, MAS and ILD in the HA20 patients from this study were the first cases reported. Thus, clinical features were significantly different between families with HA20 in our study.
100	
101	HA20 was initially identified as a Behçet’s disease-like phenotype. The original description showed that all patients with HA20 had recurrent aphthous stomatitis and genital ulcers [13]. However, not all patients included in our study and other studies developed some Behçet’s disease-like phenotypes [14–17], even if some patients included in our study and other studies did not have a Behçet’s disease-like phenotype [15–17]. Thus, HA20 is a very heterogeneous disease. Patients presenting with Behçet’s-like disease or other features of autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease starting in early childhood should be screened for the TNFAIP3 mutation, especially if there is a family history of similar symptoms, as the clinical course and response to the treatment of this genetic disorder differs from common Behçet’s disease.
102	
103	A20 functions as a negative regulator of the nuclear factor kB (NF-kB) pathway and modulates immune responses by preventing excessive activation of NF-kB in response to a variety of external stimuli [20]. It is structurally divided into two types of domains – the N-terminal Ovarian tumor (OTU) domain and the C-terminal domain containing 7 zinc finger motifs (ZnF1–ZnF7) [21]. It harbors a deubiquitination enzyme domain and activates multiple mechanisms to antagonize ubiquitination upstream of the NF-kB essential modulator (NEMO), a regulatory subunit of the IkB kinase (IKK) complex [4]. The IKK complex has 2 catalytic subunits (IKKa and IKKb) and a subunit that regulates the canonical NF-kB pathway (NEMO/IKKg). The IKK regulates the noncanonical pathway by IKKa [22]. The ubiquitin-induced recruitment of A20 to NEMO can downregulate IKK activation by blocking IKK phosphorylation. On activation, IKK phosphorylates the inhibitory IkBa protein, leading to its degradation and dissociation from NF-kB, after which it translocates to the nucleus [23]. Hence, A20 deficiency leads to the activation of the NF-kB pathway. Both a mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene in the N-terminal domain or the C-terminal domain can cause the loss of A20 function [14–17]. Approximately 10 different disease-causing mutations of the TNFAIP3 gene have been reported in various populations (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/, last updated April, 2018). In our study, WES revealed that a heterozygous c.559C > T(p.Q187X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene cosegregates with the disease in three patients of family 1. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, but it was reported by other study [16]. By sequence analysis in family 1, we found that P3 had this de novo mutation and transmitted it to his children. Interestingly, the three patients had the same genotype of the TNFAIP3 gene but had different phenotypes. The heterozygous c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene was detected by WES and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in family 2. Sequence analysis in family 2 showed that the p.R87X mutation is a de novo mutation, where a nonsense mutation leads to the truncation of A20. The p.R87X mutation was first reported in our study. The p.Q187X and p.R87X mutations are both located in OUT domains, which controlled NF-κB signaling by deubiquitinating receptor-interacting protein (RIP) 1, RIP2 and TNF receptor-associated factor (TRAF) [24].
104	
105	Here, we provide four HA20 patients with novel features of considerable existing evidence implicating novel mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene. Our study expands the phenotype and genotype spectrum of HA20.
106	
107	HA20 is a new autoinflammatory disease caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in TNFAIP3. These mutations cause insufficient DUB activity of A20 and lead to an increased NF-κB signaling and phosphorylation of c-Jun N-terminal kinase and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs). Clinical features were significantly different between families with HA20, even between numbers with the same TNFAIP3 mutation.

12	BackgroundThe association between mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene and a new autoinflammatory disease (called A20 haploinsufficiency, HA20) has recently been recognized. Here, we describe four patients with HA20 from two unrelated Chinese families.Case presentationA total of four patients from two families were included. The average age at onset was 5.9 years. All patients had no signs of eye or skin problems, such as uveitis, rash, folliculitis and dermal abscess. Prior to the recognition of HA20, P1 was diagnosed with SLE, liver fibrosis and hypothyroidism. She also had no oral, genital or perineal ulcers. P2 was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease and inflammatory bowel disease-related arthritis (IBD-RA). He had a perianal abscess but no oral or genital ulcers. P3, the father of P1 and P2, only had mild oral ulcers, arthralgia, and archosyrinx. P4 was diagnosed with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) and interstitial lung disease (ILD). Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed in two families. WES revealed heterozygous c.559C > T in the TNFAIP3 gene in P1, P2 and P3, while the c.259C > T mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene was identified in P4. The c.259C > T mutations is novel.ConclusionHA20 had a different phenotype between families and even between family members with the same mutation. Liver fibrosis, hypothyroidism, ILD and MAS in the patients with HA20 were first reported in this study. 103	A20 functions as a negative regulator of the nuclear factor kB (NF-kB) pathway and modulates immune responses by preventing excessive activation of NF-kB in response to a variety of external stimuli [20]. It is structurally divided into two types of domains – the N-terminal Ovarian tumor (OTU) domain and the C-terminal domain containing 7 zinc finger motifs (ZnF1–ZnF7) [21]. It harbors a deubiquitination enzyme domain and activates multiple mechanisms to antagonize ubiquitination upstream of the NF-kB essential modulator (NEMO), a regulatory subunit of the IkB kinase (IKK) complex [4]. The IKK complex has 2 catalytic subunits (IKKa and IKKb) and a subunit that regulates the canonical NF-kB pathway (NEMO/IKKg). The IKK regulates the noncanonical pathway by IKKa [22]. The ubiquitin-induced recruitment of A20 to NEMO can downregulate IKK activation by blocking IKK phosphorylation. On activation, IKK phosphorylates the inhibitory IkBa protein, leading to its degradation and dissociation from NF-kB, after which it translocates to the nucleus [23]. Hence, A20 deficiency leads to the activation of the NF-kB pathway. Both a mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene in the N-terminal domain or the C-terminal domain can cause the loss of A20 function [14–17]. Approximately 10 different disease-causing mutations of the TNFAIP3 gene have been reported in various populations (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/, last updated April, 2018). In our study, WES revealed that a heterozygous c.559C > T(p.Q187X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene cosegregates with the disease in three patients of family 1. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, but it was reported by other study [16]. By sequence analysis in family 1, we found that P3 had this de novo mutation and transmitted it to his children. Interestingly, the three patients had the same genotype of the TNFAIP3 gene but had different phenotypes. The heterozygous c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene was detected by WES and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in family 2. Sequence analysis in family 2 showed that the p.R87X mutation is a de novo mutation, where a nonsense mutation leads to the truncation of A20. The p.R87X mutation was first reported in our study. The p.Q187X and p.R87X mutations are both located in OUT domains, which controlled NF-κB signaling by deubiquitinating receptor-interacting protein (RIP) 1, RIP2 and TNF receptor-associated factor (TRAF) [24].

Here, we describe four patients with HA20 from two unrelated Chinese families.Case presentationA total of four patients from two families were included. The average age at onset was 5.9 years. 103	A20 functions as a negative regulator of the nuclear factor kB (NF-kB) pathway and modulates immune responses by preventing excessive activation of NF-kB in response to a variety of external stimuli [20]. It is structurally divided into two types of domains – the N-terminal Ovarian tumor (OTU) domain and the C-terminal domain containing 7 zinc finger motifs (ZnF1–ZnF7) [21]. It harbors a deubiquitination enzyme domain and activates multiple mechanisms to antagonize ubiquitination upstream of the NF-kB essential modulator (NEMO), a regulatory subunit of the IkB kinase (IKK) complex [4]. The IKK complex has 2 catalytic subunits (IKKa and IKKb) and a subunit that regulates the canonical NF-kB pathway (NEMO/IKKg). The IKK regulates the noncanonical pathway by IKKa [22]. The ubiquitin-induced recruitment of A20 to NEMO can downregulate IKK activation by blocking IKK phosphorylation. On activation, IKK phosphorylates the inhibitory IkBa protein, leading to its degradation and dissociation from NF-kB, after which it translocates to the nucleus [23]. Hence, A20 deficiency leads to the activation of the NF-kB pathway. Both a mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene in the N-terminal domain or the C-terminal domain can cause the loss of A20 function [14–17]. Approximately 10 different disease-causing mutations of the TNFAIP3 gene have been reported in various populations (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/, last updated April, 2018). In our study, WES revealed that a heterozygous c.559C > T(p.Q187X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene cosegregates with the disease in three patients of family 1. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, but it was reported by other study [16]. By sequence analysis in family 1, we found that P3 had this de novo mutation and transmitted it to his children. Interestingly, the three patients had the same genotype of the TNFAIP3 gene but had different phenotypes. The heterozygous c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene was detected by WES and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in family 2. Sequence analysis in family 2 showed that the p.R87X mutation is a de novo mutation, where a nonsense mutation leads to the truncation of A20. The p.R87X mutation was first reported in our study. The p.Q187X and p.R87X mutations are both located in OUT domains, which controlled NF-κB signaling by deubiquitinating receptor-interacting protein (RIP) 1, RIP2 and TNF receptor-associated factor (TRAF) [24].

103	A20 functions as a negative regulator of the nuclear factor kB (NF-kB) pathway and modulates immune responses by preventing excessive activation of NF-kB in response to a variety of external stimuli [20]. It is structurally divided into two types of domains – the N-terminal Ovarian tumor (OTU) domain and the C-terminal domain containing 7 zinc finger motifs (ZnF1–ZnF7) [21]. It harbors a deubiquitination enzyme domain and activates multiple mechanisms to antagonize ubiquitination upstream of the NF-kB essential modulator (NEMO), a regulatory subunit of the IkB kinase (IKK) complex [4]. The IKK complex has 2 catalytic subunits (IKKa and IKKb) and a subunit that regulates the canonical NF-kB pathway (NEMO/IKKg). The IKK regulates the noncanonical pathway by IKKa [22]. The ubiquitin-induced recruitment of A20 to NEMO can downregulate IKK activation by blocking IKK phosphorylation. On activation, IKK phosphorylates the inhibitory IkBa protein, leading to its degradation and dissociation from NF-kB, after which it translocates to the nucleus [23]. Hence, A20 deficiency leads to the activation of the NF-kB pathway. Both a mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene in the N-terminal domain or the C-terminal domain can cause the loss of A20 function [14–17]. Approximately 10 different disease-causing mutations of the TNFAIP3 gene have been reported in various populations (http://www.hgmd.cf.ac.uk/, last updated April, 2018). In our study, WES revealed that a heterozygous c.559C > T(p.Q187X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene cosegregates with the disease in three patients of family 1. The mutation was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, but it was reported by other study [16]. By sequence analysis in family 1, we found that P3 had this de novo mutation and transmitted it to his children. Interestingly, the three patients had the same genotype of the TNFAIP3 gene but had different phenotypes. The heterozygous c.259C > T (p.R87X) mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene was detected by WES and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in family 2. Sequence analysis in family 2 showed that the p.R87X mutation is a de novo mutation, where a nonsense mutation leads to the truncation of A20. The p.R87X mutation was first reported in our study. The p.Q187X and p.R87X mutations are both located in OUT domains, which controlled NF-κB signaling by deubiquitinating receptor-interacting protein (RIP) 1, RIP2 and TNF receptor-associated factor (TRAF) [24].

Here, we describe four patients with HA20 from two unrelated Chinese families.Case presentationA total of four patients from two families were included. The average age at onset was 5.9 years. All patients had no signs of eye or skin problems, such as uveitis, rash, folliculitis and dermal abscess.
